title: Argument centric causal intervention for cross document event coreference resolution
research_question: Can cross-document event coreference be improved by explicitly suppressing spurious trigger-word correlations and shifting model decisions toward event arguments and contextual semantics through causal and counterfactual intervention?
methodology: The paper introduces ACCI, an argument-centric causal-intervention framework built around pairwise cross-encoder ECR backbones. A structural causal model treats lexical trigger matching as a confounding influence, while counterfactual inputs mask or isolate triggers to estimate and subtract trigger-induced bias. A separate argument-aware path encodes the surrounding context without the trigger and is jointly optimized with the factual prediction objective. The method is evaluated on ECB+ and GVC, including backbone comparisons, ablations, cross-dataset generalization experiments, and qualitative case studies.

key_findings.finding: ACCI achieves a reported CoNLL F1 of 88.4 on ECB+, outperforming the compared systems on aggregate CoNLL F1 in the reported table.
ACCI reports a CoNLL F1 of 85.2 on GVC; it is competitive but is not the highest result in that table, where Chen2025 reports 85.8.
Removing both trigger-bias mitigation and context-argument enhancement reduces CoNLL F1 from 88.4 to 87.2 on ECB+ and from 79.0 to 77.6 in the corresponding GVC ablation setting.
The cross-dataset experiments report that ACCI consistently exceeds its corresponding baselines when training on ECB+ and testing on GVC or reversing the domains.
Qualitative cases demonstrate both relevant identity patterns: semantically different events can share the same trigger, and the same event can be expressed with different triggers.
The results support reducing dependence on surface lexical identity and using argument-level relational context as evidence for event identity.
The work directly studies cross-document real-world event identity, but it does not experimentally establish performance on enterprise email, workplace chat, or cross-channel work-matter continuity.

limitations: The causal treatment assumes that trigger information and argument/context information can be procedurally separated by subword masking, although their semantics can be entangled.
The counterfactual mechanism presents masked or placeholder-based inputs that differ from ordinary pretrained-model inputs.
The framework assumes that spurious trigger effects and causal semantic effects can be decomposed sufficiently for the proposed adjustment.
The authors identify document-level topic bias as a potential confounder not handled by the current model.
The GVC discussion notes limitations in explicitly modeling document-level event-chain structure.
The experiments use ECB+ and GVC rather than enterprise email or conversational workplace corpora.
Multilingual, multimodal, noisy social-media, news, and conversational settings are identified as future extensions rather than demonstrated capabilities.
raw_claims: Cross-document event coreference asks whether mentions in different documents refer to the same real-world occurrence.
The authors argue that pairwise models can learn spurious associations between trigger-word similarity and coreference labels.
ACCI represents trigger matching as a confounding influence in a structural causal model.
The counterfactual module evaluates predictions after altering or withholding trigger information.
The argument-aware path represents the event context while excluding the trigger.
Training combines the ordinary factual coreference objective with an argument-focused semantic objective.
Inference combines the factual score, an argument-centric score, and a correction for trigger-induced bias.
ACCI reports 88.4 CoNLL F1 on ECB+.
ACCI reports 85.2 CoNLL F1 on GVC.
Ablations reduce performance when trigger-bias mitigation or argument enhancement is removed.
Cross-domain experiments favor ACCI over corresponding baseline models.
Case studies show that identical trigger words need not indicate identical events.
Case studies also show that different trigger words can describe the same event.
The authors identify simplifying causal assumptions and document-level topic bias as unresolved limitations.
